Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Evan, a 29-year-old European American Coast Guard service member, came to treatment after months of feeling unsettled by a mugging that had happened on his way home from an evening shift. He had been walking from the parking lot toward the apartment he shared with his girlfriend when two men stepped out near the dim edge of the lot, one close enough to catch the reflection of a knife blade before it flashed away. The details of what followed never settled into a single story in his mind. When he tried to explain it, he found himself stopping and restarting, saying that he could remember “bits,” but not in a way that made sense from beginning to end. He could picture the hood of one man’s sweatshirt, the scrape of his shoes on the pavement, the cold feel of his own keys in his hand, and then nothing that linked those pieces together. He had come to believe that the event sat in him in a different form than ordinary memory, because whenever he tried to put it into words, the scene seemed to break apart before he could speak it.

In the immediate aftermath, Evan told no one at work what had happened beyond a brief report, and at home he became frustrated with himself for not being able to describe it more clearly. His girlfriend would ask what the men had looked like, what they had said, whether he had seen where they went, and he would stare past her, embarrassed by how little he could give her. Sometimes he could recall a fragment with surprising sharpness, only to feel completely numb as if it had happened to somebody else, not to him. Those moments were especially disorienting because the fear in the memory did not always come with the memory itself; instead, the scene would arrive in detached pieces, stripped of the feeling that should have gone with it, leaving him with the uneasy sense that his own mind was withholding the story from him.

For a while he tried to push through it by returning to his routine, but the absence of a coherent recollection made the event feel unresolved, as if it were still sitting open and unfinished. He started avoiding any situation that might force him to think about the mugging in one solid line, which at home meant changing the subject whenever his girlfriend asked about that night and at work meant keeping conversations practical and brief when colleagues brought up security incidents or patrols in poorly lit areas. The parking lot where he had been attacked remained part of his daily life, and each time he crossed it after a late shift he felt the same internal snag: the place was ordinary, yet it seemed to hold too many loose pieces of the event for him to trust his own mind there. If he caught a glimpse of someone loitering near the cars or heard footsteps approaching from behind, his attention would lock onto the scene with a strained, searching quality, because he was always trying to make the scattered fragments line up into something he could understand.

The more he found himself staring back at that night in his mind, the more draining the whole experience became. He began to dread being asked to recount it, not because he wanted to forget, but because every attempt left him feeling more cut off from himself and more aware of how partial the memory remained. At home, his girlfriend noticed that he was quieter and less present, especially after a late watch, and he found himself withdrawn rather than risk another clumsy effort to explain something he could not organize. The mugging had taken on an almost private, sealed quality in his mind: he knew it happened, he knew it frightened him, but the memory would not stay in one piece long enough for him to tell it in a way that felt true. That inability to narrate it became one of the things he hated most, because it left him with the sense that he could not fully account for what had happened to him.

He eventually sought help after realizing that the broken, wordless quality of the memory was keeping the event alive in a way he could not control, and that each attempt to force the pieces together only left him more shaken and ashamed. What he wanted most was to be able to remember the mugging without feeling hollowed out by it, and what frightened him most was that the fragments would never fit together well enough for him to feel like the night belonged to the past rather than to him.
